Q: Simple description of worker and I/O threads in .NET A:

.NET threads work as parts of a thread pool.

Normally, when a thread is created, it's given a pointer to the function it needs to run. It runs this function and terminates when the function returns.

When the .NET thread pool creates its threads, the functions these threads run, normally, never return (except when the application exits or the pool wants to scale down the number of threads).

At the bottom level, these functions run something in a loop. This "something" gives them units of work. Once the thread gets a unit of work, it executes it, and returns to the loop.

It looks something like this (in pseudocode):

void ThreadRunner() {
    while (!needToTerminateThisThread()) {
        Action unitOfWork = PseudocodeForGetNextUnitOfWork();
        unitOfWork();
    }
}

(To reiterate, PseudocodeForGetNextUnitOfWork is not a real function in .NET, it's pseudocode.)

It's a blocking method, and the thread is in Wait state before it returns.

What exactly PseudocodeForGetNextUnitOfWork does, depends on the type of the thread:

  1. Worker threads wait on a semaphore that is signaled when a unit of work is posted by ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem.
  2. I/O threads wait on an I/O completion port that is signaled by the kernel when asynchronous I/O happens

Now, to your questions.

Although method ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads returns number of available threads of both types, it seems there is no public API to schedule work for I/O thread.

An I/O thread gets work when the port gets a completion packet. To make it (eventually) happen, you can do either of two things:

  1. Bind a handle to the port by calling ThreadPool.BindHandle. When the handle gets I/O, the kernel send a completion packet to the port.
  2. Send the completion packet directly to the port by calling ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueNativeOverlapped

These methods are rarely called directly by applications. They're usually wrapped in library calls.

You can only manually create worker thread in .NET?

You can, but it's rarely the case that you need it.

Threads are expensive, and you want to reuse them. That's exactly what the pool does. You post units or work into the pool by calling ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem or numerous wrappers around it (e.g. Task.Run). One of the pre-created threads in the pool will pick it up in its loop and execute.

It seems that single I/O thread can monitor multiple I/O operations. Is it true?

Yes, it's true. There's a single I/O port per application (or AppDomain in .NET Framework). Windows allows binding multiple handles to a single port. The lowermost part of the I/O thread stack is a loop that repeatedly calls GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx.

When it returns, the thread reconciles the completion packet with the continuation (the unit of work it should perform on completion), and executes it.

If so, why ThreadPool has so many available I/O threads by default?

The continuation will, of course, tie up the I/O thread when it's executing. If it's long, the thread won't return to the loop until the continuation completes.

If it's a single thread, and it's tied up, your application won't be processing any I/O until the thread is done with the continuation.

In some texts I read that callback, triggered after I/O operation completion is performed by I/O thread. Is it true? Isn’t this a job for worker thread, considering that this callback is CPU operation?

It's true, and that's something libraries should pay attention to.

A common wisdom is to do the bare minimum of processing in the I/O thread, and reschedule the bulk of the work to a worked thread.

It's not a magic pill, though, because rescheduling isn't free. High-performance I/O-intensive libraries do a lot of fine-tuning to distribute the work between I/O and worker threads.

Latest versions of .NET Core, for instance, reschedule socket I/O straight to the worker threads, unless you disable this behavior by setting the environment variable DOTNET_SYSTEM_NET_SOCKETS_INLINE_COMPLETIONS. .NET Framework doesn't do that, and neither did earlier versions of .NET Core for Windows.

Some libraries (e.g. MongoDB driver for C#) are infamous for performing CPU-heavy operations of deserializing BSON documents in I/O threads, which hogs the threads and hurts I/O performance in high-load environments.

Other libraries (e.g. earlier versions of StackExchange.Redis) are similarly infamous for the way they calculate network latency and throw timeout exceptions, which includes the rescheduling time and can generate false timeouts.

It's always a matter of tradeoff.

To be more specific – do ASP.NET asynchronous pages use I/O threads?

Yes, they indirectly do. Necessarily, to read and write the request and the response, and, optionally, to process them.

What exactly is performance benefit in switching I/O work to separate thread instead of increasing maximum number of worker threads?

One I/O thread can handle units of work (continuations) scheduled by thousands different handles (sockets, files, synchronization primitives etc.), as long as you keep them short enough.

Threads are expensive to create and aren't free to maintain.

A thousand threads, each waiting for its individual handle, on average, have worse overall performance and consume more resources than one I/O thread waiting for a completion port with a thousand handles bound to it.

Q: Implementing toy model as linear programming problem A:

You can't simultaneously respect all of your constraints and exactly balance relative increase in factory output. So you need to make up your mind about what to give up. One (seemingly) reasonable compromise is to minimise the maximal relative change:

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import milp, Bounds, LinearConstraint

baseline = np.array((
    (80, 20),
    (20, 40),
    (10, 5),
))

# Variables: A foo, A bar, B foo, B bar, C foo, C bar; max rel change

'''
Ignore "minimize the relative change in output per factory"
Implement: distribute the change in output per factory as best as possible
Minimise the maximum relative change in factory output.
'''
cost = (0,0, 0,0, 0,0, 1)

# Factories cannot reduce their output.
bounds = Bounds(lb=np.concatenate((baseline.ravel(), (0,))))

# increase the total output of foo and bar system by 50 and 25.
new_output = baseline.sum(axis=0) + (50, 25)
increase_constraint = LinearConstraint(
    A=(
        (1,0, 1,0, 1,0,  0),
        (0,1, 0,1, 0,1,  0),
    ), lb=new_output, ub=new_output,
)

'''
The ratio of foo and bar per factory is fixed (e.g. factory A produces 80 units of foo per 20 units of bar).
foo/bar = foo'/bar': foo' = bar'(foo/bar)   foo' - bar'(foo/bar) = 0
'''
ratios = baseline[:, 0]/baseline[:, 1]
ratio_constraint = LinearConstraint(
    A=(
        (1, -ratios[0],  0,0,  0,0,  0),
        (0,0,  1, -ratios[1],  0,0,  0),
        (0,0,  0,0,  1, -ratios[2],  0),
    ), lb=0, ub=0,
)

'''
distribute the change over factories:
the maximal relative change must be at least the rel change of every factory
-a'0/(a0 + a1) - a'1/(a0 + a1) + relmax >= 0
'''
coef = -1/baseline.sum(axis=1)
distribution_constraint = LinearConstraint(
    A=(
        (coef[0], coef[0], 0,0, 0,0, 1),
        (0,0, coef[1], coef[1], 0,0, 1),
        (0,0, 0,0, coef[2], coef[2], 1),
    ), lb=0,
)

result = milp(
    c=cost, bounds=bounds, integrality=0,
    constraints=(increase_constraint, ratio_constraint, distribution_constraint),
)
assert result.success

prod = result.x[:-1].reshape((-1, 2))
maxrel = result.x[-1]

print('Baseline production:')
print(baseline)
print('New production:')
print(prod)
print()

print('Baseline totals by product:')
print(baseline.sum(axis=0))
print('New totals by product:')
print(prod.sum(axis=0))
print('Increase in product:')
print(prod.sum(axis=0) - baseline.sum(axis=0))
print()

print('Baseline totals by factory:', baseline.sum(axis=1))
print('New totals by factory:', prod.sum(axis=1))
print('Relative increase by factory:')
print(prod.sum(axis=1)/baseline.sum(axis=1) - 1)
print(f'Worst relative increase: {maxrel-1:.1%}')
print()

print('Baseline product ratios:')
print(ratios)
print('New product ratios:')
print(prod[:, 0]/prod[:, 1])
print()

Q: Why is my coroutine wrapper working when I use it as a decorator but not when I use it as a wrapper? A:

We often use the "coroutine" for two different types. Unfortunately it sometimes create a confusion, but we must not mix those two types.

If we have e.g. async def af(), then af is a couroutine function. When called (with function args if necessary) it creates and returns (but does not run) an awaitable af() which is a coroutine object. The coroutine must be awaited in order to run it. Side note: if it is never awaited nor closed, asyncio will complain when cleaning up.

Here is a fixed version of exception_handler. In your program it receives coro - a coroutine object, not a coroutine function. That's why no additional arguments are applicable. The function itself is a wraper, you don't need to create an extra wrapper. If need be, implement returning the obtained value.

async def exception_handler(coro):
    try:
        await coro
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"exception occurred - {e}")
    except CancelledError:
        logger.info("cancelled")
        raise
    else:
        logger.info("completed succesfully")

Q: Node mssql: return id after SQL insertion A:

I quote from node-mssql insert returning undefined recordset:

INSERT statement doesn't return a recordset so recordset is undefined. Please see this section of the docs to learn more about how to get number of affected rows.

An option to solve this is to add a SELECT statement after your INSERT and ask for SCOPE_IDENTITY() or @@IDENTITY. That will get you the ID of the last inserted objects, i.e.:

INSERT INTO table (...) VALUES (...);
SELECT SCOPE_IDENTITY() AS id;

Q: Shmget: Invalid argument. Why do I get this error? A:

From the shmget(2) man page:

EINVAL A new segment was to be created and size < SHMMIN or size > SHMMAX, or no new segment was to be created, a segment with given key existed, but size is greater than the size of that segment.

You should check whether you still have a segment for this key using ipcs and remove it with ipcrm.

Q: How do I look into folium example data to see available columns and categories? A:

This url is incorrect because data is a folder, not file, and it doesn't have "raw" version.

If you would have url to file .csv (e.g. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-visualization/folium/refs/heads/main/examples/data/consonants_vowels.csv)

then you can read it directly with pandas and display columns.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python-visualization/folium/refs/heads/main/examples/data/consonants_vowels.csv")

print(df.columns)

And if you want all filenames then maybe it would be simpler to open page https://github.com/python-visualization/folium/tree/main/examples/data and selecte text on page and copy-paste it to local text file or to your code.

Q: Limit Google Sheet to Only Be Viewed on a Tuesday (preferably between certain hours) A:

The manageTimeAccess() function is embedded inside myFunction() which makes it unreachable from many kinds of call methods, such as buttons, custom menu items or installable triggers.

To make the function testable, unwrap the manageTimeAccess() function by removing the initial function myFunction() { line and the trailing } at the last line.
